summary: feat(core/sandbox): declare a session's input surface up front so fd 0 stays /dev/null — a non-TTY session always took a stdin pipe, so a child that branches on what fd 0 is read that pipe whether or not anyone would ever write to it (`rg pattern` with no path operand searched the stream instead of the working tree, `cat` blocked, `test -p /dev/fd/0` answered true), and `ExecOptions.Stdin`'s own doc — nil means no stdin — was not implemented by `StartSession`; `SessionSpec.Stdin` is now the only declaration: with TTY false it decides the spawn (true gets a pipe, false leaves cmd.Stdin nil so os/exec hands the child /dev/null), it is ignored for TTY where the pty master is always writable, and `Start` still never delivers `Opts.Stdin`, those bytes no longer counting as a declaration either, so a non-TTY spec carrying them without `Stdin` keeps fd 0 on /dev/null and `Write` reports NotAvailable; `Exec` is unaffected because it sets `spec.Stdin` itself before `Start` and then writes and closes, and `ExecOptions.Stdin` nil or empty both mean no input, an empty slice no longer buying the child a pipe; `SessionCapabilities.Stdin` joins TTY/Signal/Events so a caller can ask before trying, `Write` on a session that declared no input returns errdefs.NotAvailable ("session started without stdin; set SessionSpec.Stdin to stream input") instead of the ErrSessionClosed it used to return, because that is a capability the spec never asked for rather than a handle that went away, and `CloseInput` on such a session stays a no-op success so `Exec` keeps calling it unconditionally; `ExecRequest.Stdin` gives the approver the same view — `Stdin || TTY` for Start, a non-empty `ExecOptions.Stdin` for Exec — so a predicate can gate on "this command channel carries caller input"; the unix `localSession` and the windows `winSession` follow the same rules (skip `StdinPipe()` when nothing declared input, remember the decision in an `input` field for `Write`/`CloseInput`/`Capabilities`, TTY paths reporting `Stdin: true`), and `Write` snapshots `stdin` under the lock instead of reading the field from the copy goroutine that `CloseInput`/`Close` nil out concurrently, which was a data race. The tests probe the child's actual fd 0 (`test -p /dev/fd/0`, falling back to /proc/self/fd/0) rather than asking whether a write succeeded: the never-ending empty pipe, `Stdin: []byte{}` buying no pipe, declared bytes still arriving through one, the session side (declared vs undeclared, NotAvailable vs ErrSessionClosed, a TTY `CloseInput` staying NotAvailable), the approver's view, and the Windows pipe backend; the merge path that never touches Runner.Exec is pinned by decorator tests, where `WithDefaults`' Stdin fallback buys no pipe and a `cat` session has to exit on its own. feat(core/delegation): give a delegated run a declared policy channel — a delegated run gets its own session identity, so a deployment that resolves execution policy per session (sandbox mode, think level, model hint) had no way to say which policy a subagent runs under: the caller's run attributes do not reach it and `Request.Metadata` is graph input, so the subagent landed on the store's default tier and every gated command failed closed from inside a run the caller cannot inspect; `Request.Attributes` carries caller-declared run attributes onto the subagent's `Run.Attributes` via `agent.Request`, which core treats as opaque, with lineage service-owned — the service's own keys are layered over the declared ones so a delegation cannot be made to look like a different tool call, and declaring `tool.call_id` is a validation error rather than a silent override, since without an ambient call id to layer over a caller-chosen value would reach `Run.Attributes` and be stamped onto every envelope as delegation lineage — the caller's own run attributes never inherited, because deployments keep run-scoped payloads there (checkpoint recovery blobs, for instance) that must not surface inside a subagent, and the map joining identity: idempotency compares it verbatim so replaying a key under a different policy is a conflict instead of a silent reuse of the earlier (possibly wider) decision, while resume identity excludes the lineage keys because a retry is a new tool call and must still replay the parked run; nil and an empty map are equivalent, an empty value is allowed and distinct from an absent key, and blank keys plus surrounding whitespace in a key or value are validation errors because the map is compared verbatim; `WithSessionInitializer` registers a `SessionInitializer` that runs once per delegated run, after the session identity is minted and before the turn starts or resumes, which is where a deployment writes the per-session state core does not model into its own store — failing closed when the hook errors rather than running under a wider default, running on the manager-less path too wherever a `SessionProvider` minted the identity, and refusing the delegation with a validation error when it has no identity at all instead of proceeding under the store's default, so configuration that could apply its policy is unaffected while the combination that silently ran unconfined now refuses; a nil option is rejected; `delegation.WithRunAttributes` is the producer for the context-stamped channel (copy-on-write, a nil or empty map clearing an outer stamp) and the `delegate` tool copies what it carries onto every `Request` it builds, so middleware — the last seam that still sees the caller's context — is the only way in and model arguments can never widen a policy, which the tool description now says outright; a host wired from a deployment document injects both through `delegation.NewServiceFactory(opts…)`, `cloneRequest` copies the map, and the JSON contract is pinned (the `attributes` field name, omitted when empty, and the round trip); deployments that use neither seam see no behavior change, and docs/guides/sandbox.md plus docs/guides/delegation.md document both seams, which one reaches a session-keyed store, and that approval is not inherited.
